title: Credit-based flow control: the receiver decides how much may be in flight
caption: TCP windows, HTTP/2 stream windows and reactive streams' request(n) all follow this pattern.

messages.label: request(3)
messages.note: The receiver has room for 3 items, so it grants 3 credits.

messages.label: credits = 0: wait
messages.note: The sender may not send more, however much work it has. Its own buffer, or its caller, absorbs the wait.

messages.label: request(2)
messages.note: Credits come back only as fast as the receiver actually finishes work.

messages.label: item 4, item 5
messages.note: The sender's rate now matches the receiver's speed exactly, without either side knowing a number up front.

scenarios.name: Alternative: push
scenarios.summary: No credits: the sender pushes as fast as it can. Lowest latency while the receiver keeps up; once it can't, items are dropped or the receiver's buffer grows without limit.

messages.label: item 1, item 2, item 3
messages.note: No permission needed: the sender writes whenever it has work.

messages.label: item 4, item 5, item 6
messages.note: The receiver's buffer is full: it has room for 3.

messages.label: item 7, item 8
messages.note: Dropped on arrival. The sender doesn't know, and keeps going.

messages.label: or buffer all → OOM
messages.note: The other choice is to keep everything in memory, which only postpones the failure.

scenarios.name: Lost credit grant
scenarios.summary: If a credit update is lost, both sides wait for each other for ever. Real protocols re-send window updates and probe a zero window on a timer.

messages.label: request(2)
messages.note: The receiver has room again, but the grant never arrives.

messages.label: credits = 0: wait…
messages.note: The sender waits for credits; the receiver waits for items. Nothing moves: a deadlock.

messages.label: window probe (timer)
messages.note: Fix: like TCP's zero-window probe, the sender asks again after a timeout, and the receiver re-sends its current window.

scenarios.name: Slow receiver
scenarios.summary: Credits come back slowly, so the sender slows down, and its own bounded buffer fills. It then pushes back on its caller: backpressure travels hop by hop to the source.

messages.label: finish item 1 (slow)
messages.note: Each item now takes 10× longer: a slow disk.

messages.label: request(1)
messages.note: Credits trickle back one at a time, at the receiver's real speed.

messages.label: own buffer full: refuse caller
messages.note: The sender doesn't buffer without limit either. It stops reading from its own source, which slows down in turn.
